segs.t: In the North Bay, fall is the best time to plant.
The soil is still warm, the air is cooler, and winter rain does the watering. So roots grow all winter, and your plants are ready for spring and need less water next summer.
segs.label: Why It Matters
segs.title: Roots Before Summer

segs.t: Friedman's has what you need: compost, mulch, garlic, spring bulbs and veggie starts, in stock at all four stores.
segs.label: Friedman's Has It
segs.title: Everything For Fall Planting

segs.t: Before you dig, check two things: how much sun the spot gets, and how fast it drains. If water sits in a test hole overnight, you've got clay, so plan on extra compost.
segs.label: Good To Know
segs.title: Check Sun And Drainage

segs.t: Here's how it typically works. Start by working compost into the soil to loosen it up.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Work In Compost

segs.t: Then dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball, but no deeper.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Dig Wide, Not Deep

segs.t: Gently loosen any circling roots, and set the plant level with the ground.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Loosen The Roots

segs.t: Backfill, and water it in well.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Backfill And Water

segs.t: And finish with two to three inches of mulch, pulled back from the stems.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Mulch, Not Touching Stems

Feel a draft at your front door? That's heat walking out.
Gaps around a door let warm air out all winter, so your heater works harder and the room by the door never feels comfortable. Sealing it is one of the easiest energy fixes in the house.
segs.label: Why It Matters
segs.title: Stop Paying To Heat Outside

segs.t: Friedman's has everything for the job: a weatherstrip kit, a door sweep, a utility knife and rubbing alcohol.
segs.label: Friedman's Has It
segs.title: Everything To Seal A Door

segs.t: Know your frame first. Pull back the old strip. If it sits in a narrow groove, you need kerf-in weatherstripping. If it's flat, use an adhesive strip. And keep the blade pointed away from you when you trim.
segs.label: Good To Know
segs.title: Groove Or Flat Frame?

segs.t: Here's how it typically goes. Find the leaks by closing the door on a sheet of paper. If it slides out easily, the seal is weak.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: The Paper Test

segs.t: Pull out the old strip, and clean the frame with rubbing alcohol.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Clean The Frame

segs.t: Cut the new strip slightly long, and press it in, starting at a top corner.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Press In The New Strip

segs.t: Then fit a door sweep so the seal just touches the threshold, and screw it in.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Add A Door Sweep

segs.t: Do the paper test one more time. Now it should drag. That's warm air staying inside.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Test It Again

segs.t: Grab everything at any Friedman's store, order online for pickup, or book a free fifteen-minute consult with a Friedman's project pro.
Before the first big storm, take an hour and follow the water.
Storms turn small problems into leaks, puddles and soggy crawlspaces, and almost all of them come down to water that isn't moving away from the house. An hour now can save a costly repair later.
segs.label: Why It Matters
segs.title: Move Water Away

segs.t: Friedman's has your storm gear: gutter scoops, downspout extensions, a sturdy ladder and flashlights.
segs.label: Friedman's Has It
segs.title: Your Storm Prep Gear

segs.t: Safety first. Set your ladder on firm, level ground, and keep three points of contact. Never go on a wet roof, and call a licensed roofer for roof repairs.
segs.label: Good To Know
segs.title: Ladder Safety First

segs.t: Here's how it typically works. Walk around the house and note where every downspout empties.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Follow Each Downspout

segs.t: Then clean the gutters. Scoop toward you, and move the ladder instead of reaching.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Scoop The Gutters

segs.t: Flush them with a hose, to make sure every downspout drains.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Flush With A Hose

segs.t: Next, add extensions, so water lands several feet from the foundation.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Extend The Downspouts

segs.t: And stage a tarp, flashlights and fresh batteries where you can find them in the dark.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Stage Your Supplies

segs.t: Get your storm gear at any Friedman's store, or order online for pickup. Need a plan or a contractor? Book a free fifteen-minute consult with a Friedman's project pro.
Frost is coming to the valleys, and your outdoor pipes are first in line.
Water expands when it freezes, and that can split a faucet or pipe, sometimes inside the wall, where you won't see it until the thaw.
segs.label: Why It Matters
segs.title: Frozen Water Splits Pipes

segs.t: Friedman's has what you need: faucet covers, foam pipe insulation, insulation tape and hose storage.
segs.label: Friedman's Has It
segs.title: Everything To Winterize

segs.t: Before the first frost, find your main water shutoff and make sure it turns. And if a pipe ever freezes, warm it gently with a hair dryer, never an open flame.
segs.label: Good To Know
segs.title: Know Your Shutoff

segs.t: Here's how it typically works. Disconnect every hose, drain it, and store it.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Disconnect The Hoses

segs.t: Then fit an insulated cover over each outdoor faucet, so it seals against the wall.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Cover Each Faucet

segs.t: Slip foam sleeves over any exposed pipe, bends included, and tape the seams.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Insulate Exposed Pipe

segs.t: Switch your sprinkler controller to rain mode.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Rain Mode On

segs.t: And wrap the backflow preventer with an insulated cover.
segs.label: How It Works
segs.title: Wrap The Backflow
